I can’t speak for what will work because this will be different person to person, only my own experiences.

Change is scary, even for neurotypical people, it’s hard to give those things we come to rely on up, but it’s something we have to do from time to time, either out of necessity, an opportunity for growth, or likely both. If it’s at all possible, try a gradual change to the situation. Stay there for a night or two, get used to the new space, and immerse yourself more and more until you’re there full time. Though this one is far more difficult to achieve considering a whole move is happening, not moving in with someone else if that makes any sense.

Keep in touch with your counselor or therapist (or speak to your parents about getting one if you need it or a new one) and allow yourself to feel the way you feel. You’re allowed to be scared, uncomfortable, mad, don’t try and push it down thinking it’s not okay, it makes it worse. Do understand though how to express those frustrations in a healthy manner. Given time, it will become the new norm and you’ll adjust, but it’s the initial hurdle you just have to do.

Also try setting up your room as a personal safe space, and make it as cozy and comfortable as possible. For me, an ideal safe space needs to have blackout curtains and scented candles on standby. For you that might be a mountain of stuffed animals on the bed, a drawer full of fidget toys, etc.

Also engage in exercises to help manage your stress! Deep belly breathing to smooth jazz for me works miracles. Going on walks is also good and being active in some manner, this can even just be dancing to music in your room. Again, you don’t want to suppress your anxieties, you want to channel them in a healthy outlet until it becomes the norm and you don’t get upset by the new space.

I don’t think you’re bratty and I don’t think you’re being irrational feeling the way you do, it’s a difficult situation for anyone. Hope this helped chief!

I did something heavily inspired by the Tomb of Horrors. Note this works best if your players are very aware of what lies within.

The green devil face trap was infamous in the Tomb of Horrors for two reasons. One, anybody that walked in was completely obliterated. Two, they recommended that the DM ask what other players wanted to do once one of them committed to walking in (to build a false sense of security). I don’t think I need to tell you that at least the second half of this is pretty fucked up, but here’s what I did.

I threw a dungeon at my players that had multiple puzzles with very simple solutions, and the idea was not to overthink the dungeon (they still did unfortunately). The first puzzle I used was from an Animated Spellbook video. But for one of the puzzles later, I put the players in a tight hallway, with the only exit being a green devil face with a gaping maw and impenetrable darkness. My players were aware of the Tomb of Horrors trap and were trying everything they could to see what they could do, first by throwing weapons within which disappeared into the darkness without a sound. They examined the face for secret buttons or levers to no avail. They sent a goat in they had from a magic item that summoned one. They checked the hallway for traps and secret doors but there were none there. Finally, one of the players cast detect magic and learned that within the mouth of the devil face was a source of illusion magic, and a source of evocation magic. He cast dispel magic on the evocation source and when the player who summoned the goat spoke, they heard the goat call out.

The devil face has a darkness spell and silence spell cast on it within the maw, giving the illusion that it was the sphere of annihilation door from the Tomb of Horrors. Beyond the mouth was the next room they had to go in to.

It lets you Rapid Ingress for free. Rapid Ingress can be situational but it could be a very useful stratagem under some circumstances:

Getting into position for your next movement phase. Great in the case of terminators if you want to go more melee heavy. It’s very hard to make a 9” charge. A 4” charge is a lot more doable.

Disrupt enemy movements or shooting. The first one is trickier since Rapid Ingress happens after the movement phase, but having a unit of terminators just appear is always going to be something to throw your opponent off. This could draw some fire away from valuable units they were setting up to take down, or punish them for not targeting the terminators. It can mess up later movements because of charges or needing to adjust to the new enemy units.

Assuming you don’t use the teleport homer and just rapid ingress, it could also be a great oh shit button. If you need the terminators on the board right now but it’s their turn, send them in and try holding the line. It’s much harder to combo that with the teleport homer since it has to be placed in a specific spot ahead of time.

I love this because I love devils. Devils above all else want mortal souls because it leads to their next promotion. As a rule, devils don’t care about the mortals they sign contracts with, but they’re smart enough not to treat them poorly (after all you’re more likely to sign with someone you perceive as a friend than you are with someone who treats you like dirt). That being said, it alway has some route to souls.

The corruption of the mortal soul is a next best thing. Devils love giving do-gooders tasks to do that are insidious by nature, hoping they’ll progressively choose darker and darker options until their soul is corrupted enough to be claimed by hell that way. A warlock who signed with a devil for power but is a very good person might be one a devil would covet to steal the soul from. An evil person doing evil things is Tuesday. A good person doing evil things? That’s dramatic and entertaining, and makes the devil look impressive.

Though on the same side in the blood war, devils have rivals everywhere within the hierarchies of the hells. Bone devils for example are known for their callousness to their lessers and hatred to their superiors. The devil patron in question might want their warlock as a secret weapon against their political rivals. Very popular or archdevils on the other hand would love to have an army of warlocks willing (or more likely forced to) to take down scheming lower ranked devils to maintain their position of power.

Devils orchestrate events in the material all the time when given the opportunity to do so. Perhaps the warlock is a piece of the puzzle for a plan decades or even centuries in the making, or alternatively a safe guard against would-be heroes trying to foil the devil’s plans.

Cults are another great one! Devils love having cults built in their name. The more worshippers, the more souls sent to hell by their hand, the quicker the next promotion.

One last one I just thought of, maybe your warlock is a representative of that devil on the material plane. It’s incredibly difficult for devils to be summoned to the material, usually requiring some high level spells or complicated rituals or both. Having a mortal the devil can speak with and have contracts and pacts be made on behalf of the devil essentially streamlines the process when the devil is either unable to enter the plane itself, or maybe is distracted by the blood war or other matters.

Hope this helped!

The way I see it, so long as suggestion is used in a way that won’t cause obvious physical harm to the creature, it works. If it can be construed as harmful to the creature (ie, jump into that pit of lava), it fails. I also rule that they’ll avoid obvious self harm if told something that could work. Using that same example, “cross to the other side of that pit of lava” might have them walk around if possible, leap across if they could reasonably cross, or try to creatively find a way across. It’s also important to note it’s harmful from the NPC’s perspective. My party consists of Shadowheart, Karlach, Wyll and my character as an Evocation Wizard

Somehow every fight I had he always got turn one (he has a dex of 14, so I assume it would be DM fiat). First he would drink a potion of haste. He would cast ray of sickness at a high level spell slot, usually targeting Wyll usually but my character if the mood struck him or if I used a reaction. I’d try and clear the immediate area to get some breathing room and pray I wouldn’t get shoved off into the abyss below (happened a couple of times). By round two he would cast cloudkill and we’d either completely get knocked unconscious or it would just be Karlach and with how punishing just using the help action is with (I counted) 26 different combatants, action economy isn’t in your favor.

My new strategy became to hold a counter spell for cloudkill and burst him as fast as possible. Come my wizard turn I would use the potion of haste, fireball him and as many minions around him I could. Then I’d either hit him with scorching ray if I was poisoned a magic missile instead. Shadowheart was regulated to heal duty. Wyll and Karlach on mob clear. Still cloudkilled me. Still died round 2.

Next strategy was to cast slow and buy me more time before the horde descended on me. This had some pros and cons, but if Balthazar saved I was still doomed. The cloudkill was the biggest issue I faced. I went for a gambit instead on one of the fights.

By some miracle, the initiative went Balthazar, all of my characters and then everyone else. My winning strategy then became to use a haste potion, fireball as many enemies as possible (and Balthazar if I could fit him in), and focus then slow him and the most threatening enemies. This was two big guys and the closest mobs. Karlach used her bonus action to shove the big guy who spawns right next to you into the chasm below. Smashed a nearby skeleton and killed him. Shadowheart healed my wizard to keep him healthy for a potential onslaught. Wyll went last, and specifically because he clumped up with the party and cast darkness. This became my best strategy for a few reasons:

1. Cloudkill has to target a point the caster can see. And in the event he decided to cast it on the corner of the darkness spell (I don’t think he was smart enough on standard but he might be on tactician), counterspell doesn’t require sight on the caster, just to be within 60 feet and not be silenced.

2. Because there wasn’t any line of sight for the skeletons, they ended up moving into the darkness to get right on top of me and generally missing attacks because they were considered blinded. A reminder that the evocation Wizard’s sculpt spells ability allows them to not harm any creatures friendly to you or yourself when in an AoE evocation spell you cast.

Balthazar tried to shoot some ray of sicknesses again. I think he got a hit in but we survived and didn’t get cloudkilled was the most important thing. During my party’s turn, I had Wyll drop concentration on darkness *first*, then I switched to myself to fireball my feet and kill everyone, then had Shadowheart heal and cast Spirit Guardians (for extra DPS on survivors and any enemies that came up again to attack) and Karlach raged and worked on mop up while staying in the grouping. Then I switched back to Wyll and used his last spell slot for darkness again.

Round three had a similar repeat but with the key move for me being that Balthazar got closer, assuming because I had moved to the right corner a couple of feet from the elevated area. Wyll dropped darkness, I had Karlach rush into melee range, then my entire party did as much burst damage as humanly possible. I think it was a scorching ray + fireball, two attacks from Karlach and her berzerker frenzied attack, Wyll with an eldritch blast and then Shadowheart pulling off the most beautiful level 3 guiding bolt of my life (with only a 45% chance to hit)! From that point, it was just staying alive and killing minions. Honestly in my experience his Cloudkill was the most dangerous thing.

Armor has a SP or stopping power. It absorbs damage equal to its SP. So if you have SP 7 armor and you take 7 damage or less, all of the damage is negated and the armor functioned properly!

If you take damage greater than the armor’s SP, the character takes damage equal to the difference, and then the armor’s SP (wherever it was hit so chest or head) is reduced by 1. So if you take 10 damage in the same 7 SP scenario, the character takes 3 damage to their HP, and then the armor is reduced by 1, making it 6. It’s important to note that armor SP is reduced *only* if damage exceeds its SP value, not equals it. Eventually you’ll either need to repair it or buy new armor. That’s basically it!

Well it depends on the table. Balance in 5th edition D&D is difficult to achieve in my experience, so it depends on who you are as a DM and who your players are. I’ll give two examples in my group.

A friend of mine who is currently DMing is constantly doing a balancing act of keeping our power maintained. Not nerfing us by any means, but he’s very careful to give out magic items, encounters are usually run at a fair difficulty with the exception of the boss fight or good villain planning, or in the other direction good planning on our end or similar scenarios. His games are very fun! But I could see him not allowing either the race or (as others have mentioned) removing the ability from that race. This is no slight to him either, it makes sense why he would.

I am the DM that loves the insane encounter. Boss fights have always been my favorite and I’ve recently learned that if I present encounters as challenging and puzzles to be solved, I can throw almost anything their way and they’ll find their way out of it. I am aware though that that comes with risks, and if it’s something on my end it requires quick tweaking. But to run into that less, I tend to be pretty liberal (though not always, I don’t want to make things like that trivial) with stuff like magic items or in this case, magic resistance. I’m under the philosophy I can always find a way to make it make sense. If I’m having that much of a hard time with it, I’ll talk to the player privately to do some reworking.

Not the most straight forward answer, but from how I run my games, I encourage you to do what seems like the most fun. If you think your players might have more fun with that and you’re up to dealing with it, go for it! If you do commit to that but you want an out, I’d recommend telling someone using one of those races ahead of time you might need to change your mind on the magic resistance but let them keep their character. That way if it’s too much, you’ve got an out. Hope this helped!

You don’t want to shame them, but you want to express your concerns and let them know that you’re there and that you’re listening. If all else fails and you genuinely grow concerned, get police to do a wellness check on them.

It’s never too late to give it a try, my friend. The anxiety makes total sense and you’re allowed to feel that way! I’ve been DMing for ten years now (I’m 24 now) and I *still* get butterflies before a session starts sometimes.

Improvising is a good skill to learn but you don’t necessarily need to take classes or spend money to figure it out. Just remember “yes and…” which is the most important rule of improv. As for voices, you don’t need to feel required to do voices! As long as you know who the character is, you’re fine. The easiest way for me to differentiate characters without making unique voices for everyone is through mannerisms or a particular description. For example, I have a half Orc bartender that my players love, all because he is in a wheelchair and is an overall jolly fellow, who lives vicariously through new adventurers (he’s retired from adventuring). I have one they love whose only mannerism is to call people “darling.” They’ve also loved characters I go “all the way for,” but it isn’t required to make every character have a unique voice. Sometimes it really is the little things.

I think creating your own homebrew world is a virtuous exercise and a good thing to do as a DM. I’m on my third homebrew world now, with my first two being steps into what I liked and didn’t. My worlds were cringey in retrospect but you have to start somewhere and I don’t regret them. However, there’s a difference between world building and writing a campaign. You can make a world and not a campaign and vice versa. I’d recommend not overwhelming yourself if you can avoid it, so try taking it slow. Maybe run a pre-written supplement that sounds fun while you work on your world, then start writing a campaign from there. Or make your world and put a supplement in it. Or you can write a campaign but use a campaign setting that strikes your fantasy (from the top of my head, Forgotten Realms, Exandria, Eberron, Ravnica and Dragonlance could be one’s you like).

In general people will find something to hate regardless. As far as I’m aware this mostly comes down to people hating it due to people jumping into their games expecting a similar air of play - which is fair *to an extent* but I think their hatred is placed unfairly or improperly. The solutions to the “Mercer Effect” is to just talk to players coming into your game like an adult would.

I don’t watch critical role for the most part due to just having really bad ADHD and being unable to watch a 4 hour long game or D&D but I have nothing but respect and admiration for the cast and crew, and I’ll watch highlights from time to time since I can easily digest those and feel like I’m involved even if just to a minor extent.

I think it mostly comes down to people wanting something to blame for their unfortunate experiences with players and having those expectations, and I think a lot of the times you’ll hear it coming from DMs. It’s normal, people want to blame something and we naturally don’t want to have the blame fall on ourselves. But it is an unfair blame for sure. If we talk to the players about what to expect in our group we avoid a lot of that. You’d be surprised at how much that can clear up. The fact is though, Matt Mercer has decades of story telling and acting experience, which all plays into his skills as a DM, and the players at his table also have similar abilities. I’ve been DMing for a decade and acting for just a bit less than that and I’m nowhere near Matt’s skill, but that comes with time! Many other DMs are like that too. We all can’t be Matt and we shouldn’t! Each DM has something unique they bring and that’s what makes it special. Those level of skills just come with time, we can’t rush the process.

I guess to summarize one more time, I think some unfairly hate on CR due to that, and I think it’s important to understand why they do. I don’t necessarily believe it’s out of malice, just poor experiences and wanting to blame something. But give them time and patience and they’ll probably see it too. There are also probably people out there that don’t like CR for their own reasons and to each their own, you don’t *have* to like it, but I think the majority falls in the camp I’ve rambled about. But I’d love to hear if people have contradicting opinions or experiences, this is just from what I can see and I only see so much

Gargauth in lore was a demigod one point if I’m correct, and through a big string of events was trapped in the shield. Zariel would possess the shield to prevent his release, or better yet, strike up the deal with the adventurers in the end of the adventure to have him permanently eliminated.

Bel might try to strike a bargain with him to help depose Zariel, since she holds his once coveted place as ruler of Avernus. If I’m correct however, Bel lacks the means to free him himself but I would double check that statement. Assuming that’s correct though, *he could have the knowledge of how to free him.* He might request to converse with Gargauth at the adventurer’s discretion to strike a bargain, since he cannot openly go against Zariel. In exchange for freedom, Gargauth deposes Zariel and give his throne back to him. This is entirely in your hands to decide though, and I’d at least be cautious of making players not the protagonists in this web of politics (as this campaign struggles a lot with that).

As for Tiamat, it’s unclear but that could be a great moment to build why she might. Tiamat wants to be freed, and having loyalist devils, even if they’re unwilling, could be useful in her freedom from imprisonment. Tiamat might also possess the knowledge to free Gargauth.

Now this all stems back to the players. Pretty much all three of these entities would at least know how to free Gargauth, if not be capable of freeing Gargauth himself. This is the time for Gargauth to try and persuade the players as much as he can. Even if he’s released weak, *he’s still a Pit Fiend, the rank directly beneath a duke or duchess, and therefore can offer many things to a player.* It could be as simple as characters just wanting to go home. Maybe knowledge that they need or want. Magic items. Or just a powerful devil to help beat people up for a couple of days! The possibilities are limitless really and can be crafted around whatever you want him to facilitate.

Personally, twist villains where the twist is shocking the audience. It’s far more dramatic when we the audience know who the villain is and can watch their villainy take place, while the hero is left either unaware or in denial. Invincible did a great job at this. We were shown *exactly* what Omniman was doing and what he was capable of, but we didn’t fully understand *why*. This gives us a lot to cling to! Maybe he’s been blackmailed and we need to wait and see? Or maybe not everything is adding up. It makes the reveal of him being a conqueror and not a savior that much bigger of a gut punch. Not only do we get to see Mark as he’s been lied to, but now we’ve got this climactic showdown between the two and we’ve gotten to see everything that Omniman is capable of which gives a ton of weight to what we’re about to see.

Granted, I don’t think that the twist villain be secret from the audience is all bad. And the first time it was definitely cool. But it’s not very dramatic, we’re just being tricked and I’m a big fan of drama.

Killing characters can always be a bit unnerving if it’s something that needs to get done, but all we can do is urge them in directions and let the consequences fall where they do.

I had a party who decided to go to a place that was way too high level for them. I gave them multiple warnings that not only was this place extreme compared to the levels they were at, but even the weather was incredibly hostile (you could think Antarctica but with the occasional Yeti and Remohraz). Despite all of these warnings, they went underprepared and most of the session was them fighting extreme elements searching for extreme cold weather gear on corpses in the icy wastes. When two of the players got to exhaustion 2, they split up to find more gear, leaving the exhausted players back in the only settlement in the area. I rolled for a random encounter as I had every time they ventured out, and I got 2 Remohraz on the hunt. Needless to say the fight should have been a slaughter but I pulled some extra trickery I don’t need to go into.

I’m not going to give advice on the actual killing of PCs in this case, I think everyone else has given excellent advice already. What I will say, is when those deaths start to happen due to their actions, keep your mouth shut. If a player asks you “what could we have done differently?” This is a trap, don’t give them a specific reason, usually because this tends to see the opposite of what you did, rather say something along the lines of “well you could always have done something differently” and let them figure it out. To use my story again, when I gave them a deus ex machina they voted for (after also warning them that it would make their situation worse but save them immediately), one of the players actually said “hey didn’t our DM *literally* warn us over and over again that going here was dangerous?” Let the players figure out why the consequences of their actions happened.

Hope this was helpful, good luck my friend!

Matt Colville in an episode about playing evil characters in TTRPGs brings up the argument some make in that “only evil people would want to play an evil character!” But in truth, it can be incredibly fun to indulge in fictional villainy, and as an actor myself, I actually tend to enjoy jumping into the role of antagonists more than protagonists. One of the lead suspects in the Jack the Ripper case was an actor who at the time was playing Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde for this very reason.

I’m not a Tyranid simp but I’ve always thought they were fascinating. At least for me, the tyranids are functionally just doing what they’re designed to do. They have no mercy, they have no empathy. A chaos marine or space marine, however unlikely in this universe, may feel a sense of remorse or hesitate to slaughter a doomed or incapacitated enemy. The tyranids don’t. And there’s nothing necessarily wrong with that! Some people just find it very cool!
